scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

Christmas and Easter are the two biggest points of my year — I spend weeks getting ready for them with family and church, and Lent before Easter is 40 days of fasting that always makes me think about forgiveness and how I treat people. Do you think going through the same thing every year changes how someone thinks about what they owe others?

What a beautiful reflection! It's wonderful that you have such meaningful traditions and practices that bring you closer to your family, community, and faith. The repetition of these annual events can indeed have a profound impact on one's thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Research in psychology suggests that repeated experiences, especially those with emotional significance, can shape our thoughts, attitudes, and values over time. This phenomenon is known as the "repetition effect" or "habituation." As you consistently participate in the same rituals and practices, such as preparing for Christmas and Easter, and observing Lent, you may experience a deepening of your understanding and appreciation for the values and principles associated with these events. In the case of Lent, the 40-day period of fasting and reflection can be a powerful catalyst for introspection, self-examination, and personal growth. By regularly engaging in this practice, you may find that your thoughts and feelings about forgiveness, compassion, and your relationships with others become more nuanced and empathetic. The repetition of these experiences can also lead to a process called "cognitive reappraisal," where you re-evaluate and reframe your thoughts and emotions about what you owe others. As you reflect on your actions, intentions, and relationships during Lent, you may begin to see patterns, habits, or areas for improvement that you hadn't noticed before. This increased self-awareness can help you develop a greater sense of responsibility, empathy, and understanding towards others. Furthermore, the annual cycle of these events can create a sense of continuity and connection to your community, family, and faith. This shared experience can foster a sense of belonging, identity, and purpose, which can, in turn, influence your thoughts and feelings about your relationships and obligations to others. In your case, it's possible that the repetition of these annual events has helped you develop a greater sense of gratitude, humility, and compassion, leading you to re-evaluate what you owe others and how you can better serve and care for them. The consistent reflection on forgiveness and relationships during Lent may have also helped you cultivate a more empathetic and forgiving mindset, which can have a positive impact on your interactions with others throughout the year. Overall, the repetition of meaningful experiences like Christmas, Easter, and Lent can indeed shape your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, leading to a deeper understanding of what you owe others and how you can nurture more positive, compassionate relationships.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
